Recent research led by Dr. Laura E. Crotty Alexander of the University of California, San Diego, has revealed that cigarette smoke not only damages human health but also actively fuels the virulence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, specifically Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Published in the journal *Infection and Immunity*, the study demonstrates that exposure to cigarette smoke extract significantly alters the cell walls of MRSA, making the bacteria more aggressive and difficult to kill.

When macrophages attempt to engulf the bacteria, they struggle to kill smoke-exposed MRSA. Furthermore, smoke-exposed MRSA adheres more effectively to human cells, facilitating invasion. In animal models, MRSA exposed to cigarette smoke caused significantly higher mortality in mice compared to non-exposed bacteria. The study also compared cigarette smoke to e-cigarette vapor, finding that while vapor also alters bacterial structure, cigarette smoke induces a 10 times greater change in the cell wall. These findings suggest that cigarette smoke creates a dual threat by harming the smoker's immune system while simultaneously empowering the pathogens they encounter.
answers: Superbugs such as MRSA are already bad enough. But it turns out that something can make them even nastier: cigarette smoke. "We already know that smoking cigarettes harms human respiratory and immune cells, and now we've shown that, on the flipside, smoke can also stress out invasive bacteria and make them more aggressive," says lead author Laura Crotty Alexander of UC San Diego. A recent study led by University of Toulouse researcher Young-Ho Eom utilized a Google-inspired algorithm to analyze Wikipedia and determine the most influential figures across 24 language editions. The study aimed to measure influence by analyzing the web of links connecting articles, rather than simply counting views or citations. 

The initial results were surprising, identifying Carl Linnaeus, the 18th-century Swedish naturalist known as the "Father of Taxonomy," as the most influential person in the world. The researchers attribute this to a quirk in Wikipedia's structure: because Linnaeus created the system for classifying species, he is linked to from nearly every page that mentions a scientific name, from the domestic cat to the Asian elephant. 

To address this bias, the team developed a second metric called CheiRank, which measures outgoing links rather than incoming ones. When combined, the final "2DRank" algorithm placed Frank Sinatra at the top of the list for the English-language edition, followed by Michael Jackson and Pope Pius XII. The study also revealed that Wikipedia tends to highlight local historical figures and that most important figures are male and born in Western countries after the 17th century.
answers: Using methods borrowed from Google, a group of researchers has analyzed all Wikipedia pages and determined that, at least on the English language version of the site, Frank Sinatra is the world's most important person. Second place goes to Michael Jackson, and third to Pope Pius XII. When factoring in all 24 language editions of the online encyclopedia, the team found that Adolf Hitler ranked the most important person, while Michael Jackson was again second and Madonna third, reports the Guardian. "Our analysis shows that most important historical figures across Wikipedia language editions are born in western countries after the 17th century, and are male," the authors write. The researchers combined two algorithms to reach these conclusions. First, Google's PageRank algorithm, which determines a page's importance based on how many other pages link to it. In using PageRank on Wikipedia, the most important person in the world was 18th-century Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus, likely because the pages of organism after organism link back to the "father of taxonomy." So the researchers added an algorithm called CheiRank, which determines importance based on the number of outgoing links, the thought being that an important person would himself be connected to other important people, things, and events. Using the two together—an approach they dubbed 2DRank—no one beat out Frank Sinatra on English pages or Adolf Hitler across all language versions. That year, the outbreak coincided with a widespread infection of enterovirus D68 (EV-D68), leading some to believe the virus caused the paralysis. However, subsequent testing has not definitively linked EV-D68 to AFM, and no other specific pathogen has been identified. Health officials are currently investigating whether the current rise in cases is due to a new outbreak of EV-D68 or simply increased awareness and reporting. The CDC has sent out health alerts to encourage doctors to report cases promptly.

There is currently no specific treatment for AFM, though some doctors have reported that intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or steroids might help. Physical therapy is the primary intervention, and the long-term prognosis varies. While most patients do not fully recover, some, like 4-year-old Laura Carson, have shown significant improvement after intensive rehabilitation. The CDC advises the public to practice good hygiene, such as hand washing, to prevent the spread of potential viral causes.

As the scientists explain in the journal Evolution, per UT News, the sound actually comes out of the neck area after air is pushed through an esophageal pouch. On January 31, 2018, a rare celestial event will occur: a total lunar eclipse featuring a "Super Blue Moon." This event is unique as it combines a supermoon (when the moon is at its closest orbital point to Earth) with a blue moon (the second full moon of a month) and a total eclipse. Such a combination has not happened for over 150 years, with the next occurrence expected in 2028. The moon will turn a reddish "blood moon" hue due to atmospheric refraction.

The Virtual Telescope Project will partner with astrophotographers worldwide to livestream the event. The stream will begin at 11:30am UTC from Australia and will also feature the Super Blue Moon rising over Rome at 4:00pm UTC. Viewers in North America will need to wake up early, as the eclipse begins at 4:51am PST and ends at 6:48am EST. The event is part of a trilogy of supermoons, with the first appearing on December 3, 2017, and the second on New Year's Day. The third and final supermoon is the most recommended for viewing due to its special combination of events.

For the first time since 1866, a total lunar eclipse will occur with the blue moon, or second full moon of the month, which—like the one visible on New Year's Day—will also be a supermoon. Got all that? When the moon is at or near the closest point to Earth in its orbit (aka, a supermoon), it appears 14% bigger and 30% brighter than full moons that occur at the farthest point in the moon's orbit, though the moon will lose brightness as it enters Earth's shadow, according to NASA. Because of the way Earth's atmosphere bends light, the eclipsed moon will take on a reddish hue, something often referred to as a blood moon, making this rare celestial event "a super blue blood moon eclipse," according to the Miami Herald. The next blue moon eclipse won't occur until 2028. The eclipse will last for 3.5 hours, with the total eclipse stretching for 77 minutes, reports Sky & Telescope. Those along the Pacific Rim from Alaska and northwestern Canada to central and eastern Asia, Indonesia, New Zealand, and Australia will get the best view of totality during the middle of the night. However, partial phases of the eclipse should be visible under a clear sky in central North America, western Asia, India, the Middle East and eastern Europe, per Space.com. North American viewers should look up as the moon sets on the morning of Jan. 31, while those on the opposite side of the world should see a partial eclipse as the moon rises. Not in an ideal viewing area? The Virtual Telescope plans to livestream the total eclipse from Australia, which you can watch here, per Quartz. (Bogus glasses damaged a solar eclipse viewer's eyes.)
